qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Lecture four. Selection and operators. This is about who gets to breed, and how children are made.
In a generational algorithm, the whole population is replaced by children. Here the best, at zero point nine, is lost.
Generational: the whole population is replaced.
Elitism fixes that. It copies the best across unchanged, and only the others are replaced.
Elitism copies the best across unchanged.
In steady-state, a single child arrives, and it replaces the weakest member.
Steady-state: one child replaces the weakest.
A child with fitness zero point five arrives. Two rules decide which member it replaces.
A child with fitness 0.5 arrives.
The first-weaker rule scans from the left, and stops early. The weakest rule checks all five.
First weaker stops early. Weakest checks all five.
So the first-weaker rule leaves the zero point one alive, which keeps more variety.
The 0.1 survives: more variety is kept.
Three populations of twelve run for eight generations. Each row is a generation, and orange cells are copies of the best.
Each row is a generation. Orange = copies of the best.
Only selection acts here. There is no mutation, and no crossover.
Only selection acts: no mutation, no crossover.
Random picking is too weak, and nothing improves. Always picking the best is too strong. Tournament selection sits in between.
Too weak: no progress. Too strong: one copy wins.
Roulette selection gives each individual a slice of the wheel, sized by its fitness.
Each slice is sized by fitness.
The bigger the slice, the likelier the pick. Fitness two, three and five give twenty, thirty and fifty percent.
The bigger the slice, the likelier the pick.
Now one superfit individual joins, with fitness one hundred. It takes ninety-nine percent of the wheel.
One superfit individual takes 99% of the wheel.
So it is picked again and again, and the rest hardly get a turn.
It is picked again and again.
With roulette, the superfit individual takes ninety-nine percent.
Roulette: the superfit takes 99%.
Rank selection replaces each fitness with its rank. Only the order counts, not the gaps.
Rank: only the order counts, not the gaps.
The exponent b turns the pressure up or down. A bigger b favours the top ranks, and a b of zero makes every pick equal.
The exponent b turns the pressure up or down.
Tournament selection draws a few at random, and the better one wins. Here we draw two.
Draw two at random. The better one wins.
The overall best was not even drawn, so it cannot win this time.
The best was not even drawn.
A bigger t means tougher competition, because more are drawn.
A bigger t means tougher competition.
So the best wins more and more often as t grows.
The best wins more often as t grows.
Each encoding needs its own kind of mutation. A bit is flipped, an integer is re-rolled, and a real number is nudged.
Each encoding needs its own kind of mutation.
A tour is different. Re-rolling a city breaks it: D appears twice, and J is lost.
Re-rolling a tour breaks it: D twice, J lost.
Swapping two genes is safe. Every city still appears exactly once.
Swapping two genes keeps every city once.
Take two parents with eight genes each. One-point crossover cuts once, and swaps the tails.
One cut: swap the tails.
Two-point crossover cuts twice, and swaps the middle part.
Two cuts: swap the middle part.
Uniform crossover uses a mask. Wherever the mask has a one, that gene is swapped.
Uniform: a 1 in the mask swaps that gene.
Now we put it together, and evolve a picture. The fitness is the number of pixels that match, and blank pixels count too.
Fitness: pixels that match, blank ones too.
Two recipes race to copy a heart. One is steady-state, the other is generational. Both rely on mutation.
Two recipes race. Both rely on mutation.
In this run, algorithm one gets there first, after just over three thousand evaluations. Algorithm two needs nearly five thousand.
Algorithm 1 got there first, in this run.
Replace everyone, or only a few. The replacement rule decides who stays.
Tune the selection pressure, so it is not too weak, and not too strong.
Choose mutation and crossover that fit the encoding.
